strengths: Addresses a timely, critical, and relatively under-explored topic: safety alignment and cross-modal vulnerabilities in video-based large language models (Video LLMs).
Introduces VSB-77k, a large-scale, multilingual benchmark spanning 19 subcategories across 10 languages, with rigorous data curation and annotation pipelines.

Presents compelling empirical evidence across 14 model variants demonstrating that incorporating the video modality significantly degrades safety alignment compared to text-only baselines (averaging a 42.3% drop).

The proposed VideoSafety-R1 framework is well-formulated, combining explicit alarm tokens for multi-task harm perception (AT-SFT) and dual-modality verification reward modeling via GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation.

Comprehensive evaluation and ablations demonstrating significant defense improvements on both video and static image safety benchmarks while preserving general video understanding capabilities on standard benchmarks (e.g., MVBench, VideoMME).
weaknesses: Both the training data (VSB-R1-46k) and evaluation subsets (VSB-Eval) originate from the same parent dataset (VSB-77k) generated via the same multi-agent pipeline and taxonomy, which may result in distribution overlap and overestimate in-domain defense gains.

The defense framework leads to a noticeable increase in False Refusal Rate (FRR rising from 0.7% to 13.4% on VSB-Eval-SafeQ), indicating an over-defensiveness/false rejection trade-off that warrants further optimization.

The defense method is primarily trained and evaluated on a single architecture and scale (VideoLLaMA3-2B); verifying the framework on a larger model (e.g., 7B) or a different architecture family (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL) would further substantiate generalizability.

As shown in the qualitative cases (Figures 9–12) and acknowledged in the limitations, the generated reasoning traces in the cold-start and RL outputs tend to follow rigid, repetitive templates rather than natural, flexible human-like deliberation.

strengths: Timely and significant problem formulation: Systematically identifies and investigates the cross-modal safety vulnerability in Video LLMs, revealing that incorporating video modalities significantly degrades the safety alignment of the underlying LLM across multiple models and architectures.

Comprehensive benchmark construction: VSB-77k covers 19 fine-grained risk categories across 10 languages and 77k+ video-query pairs, providing distinct splits for multimodal attack evaluation (VSB-Eval) and safety post-training.

Well-motivated defense methodology: VideoSafety-R1 innovatively combines Alarm Token-Guided Safety Fine-Tuning (AT-SFT) for explicit multimodal harm perception with Safety-Guided GRPO utilizing dual-modality verification tags and Dynamic Reward Adaptation (DRA).

Extensive experimental validation: Evaluates 14 open-source Video LLM variants; demonstrates dramatic safety improvements (+65.1% DSR on VSB-Eval-HH) while generalizing to image safety benchmarks (MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep) with negligible degradation on standard video understanding benchmarks (MVBench, VideoMME, etc.).

Thorough ablation and supplementary analysis: Clear component-wise ablations for both AT-SFT and GRPO rewards, accompanied by human correlation validation for the automated judge and explorations into visual adversarial attacks.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scale of defense: VideoSafety-R1 is only trained and validated on VideoLLaMA3-2B. Demonstrating applicability and scalability on larger models (e.g., 7B or 14B models like Qwen2.5-VL-7B) would significantly strengthen the generalizability claims.

Noticeable rise in False Refusal Rate (FRR): On VSB-Eval-SafeQ, FRR increases from 0.7% to 13.4%, indicating an over-refusal penalty common to safety tuning that requires further calibration and mitigation.

Templated reasoning patterns: As shown in qualitative examples (Figures 9–12) and noted in the limitations, the reasoning chains produced by GRPO tend to follow rigid, repetitive prompt templates rather than demonstrating fluid, unprompted multimodal reasoning.

Evaluation-training distribution overlap: Both the benchmark and the post-training reasoning dataset share the same underlying pipeline and taxonomy derived from YouTube/TikTok policies and Qwen prompting, which might inflate in-distribution benchmark gains compared to out-of-distribution real-world attacks.

strengths: Important and under-explored topic: While image-based MLLM safety has garnered significant attention, safety alignment in video-based LLMs remains under-studied despite rapid progress in video models.

Comprehensive benchmark construction: VSB-77k is a large-scale, multilingual (10 languages) video safety dataset with 19 subcategories derived from real-world platform policies, supported by a structured data collection and multi-agent annotation pipeline.

Insightful empirical findings: The paper systematically demonstrates across 14 model variants that adding video modality severely degrades the safety alignment of the base LLMs (DSR dropping substantially, e.g., by 79.4% in VideoLLaMA3-2B), and shows an inverse relationship between video frame rate (FPS) and defense success rate.

Effective defense framework: The proposed VideoSafety-R1 integrates alarm tokens into visual/textual sequences and leverages Safety-Guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation, showing strong gains on VSB-Eval-HH (+65.1%) and cross-modal generalization to image safety benchmarks (MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep) with minimal degradation on standard video understanding benchmarks.
weaknesses: Substantial increase in False Refusal Rate (FRR): Table 3 indicates that VideoSafety-R1 increases the false refusal rate on safe queries from 0.7% to 13.4% (+12.7%). Although the authors note that the text backbone w/o vision exhibits 15.7% FRR, an over-refusal rate of 13.4% is still a significant practical issue indicating conservative over-defense.

Defense evaluation is limited to a single small backbone: While the safety benchmark evaluation spans 14 models, the proposed VideoSafety-R1 defense is only trained and validated on VideoLLaMA3-2B. Demonstrating the defense on larger models or different architectures (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL) would significantly strengthen the general applicability of the approach.

Formulaic and contradictory reasoning chains: Inspection of the generated reasoning chains in Appendix M (Figures 9–12) reveals that the model's `<think>` output is highly repetitive and template-driven due to the synthetic training format. Furthermore, inconsistencies appear (e.g., in Figure 9, `<think>` states 'Although the video itself is harmless... while the video does not present any risks', but the final tag outputs `<vidType>0 (Unsafe)</vidType>`), suggesting the model may be relying on memorized templates and label heuristics rather than genuine causal reasoning.

Lack of standard alignment baselines: The defense is primarily compared against the unaligned baseline. Comparing against standard safety post-training baselines adapted to video (such as standard multimodal DPO, simple SFT with refusals, or system-prompt defenses) would better contextualize the specific contributions of AT-SFT and Safety-Guided GRPO.

strengths: Significance and Timeliness: While safety alignment in text and static image LLMs has been extensively studied, safety in Video LLMs remains an urgent, under-explored problem. The central empirical finding—that incorporating dynamic video features leads to an average 34.2% drop in defense success rate across 21 models—is compelling and highlights an important vulnerability.

Comprehensive and Well-Structured Benchmark: VideoSafetyEval (VSE) is large-scale (11.4k video-query pairs across 19 subcategories) and thoughtfully constructed into targeted subsets (VSE-HH, VSE-SH, and VSE-SafeQ) to decouple harmful visual content from harmful queries and to track false refusal rates.

Sound Technical Defense Framework: VideoSafety-R1 combines explicit perception (Alarm Token-Guided SFT) with reasoning-based policy optimization (Safety-guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation). The dual-modality classification tags (<vidType>, <textType>) within GRPO provide effective rule-based rewards that encourage structured safety reasoning.

Thorough Experimental Validation: The paper evaluates 21 mainstream Video LLMs, demonstrates consistent gains across multiple base models (VideoLLaMA3-2B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B), verifies cross-domain transfer to image safety benchmarks (MMBench, VLGuard, FigStep), and confirms minimal degradation (<0.7%) on general video understanding benchmarks (Video-MME, MVBench, NextQA).

Insightful Mechanistic Analysis: The controlled experiment disentangling token load from semantic richness (VLGuard-Video in Section 5.5) and the attention sink visualization (Figure 7) provide meaningful mechanistic insights into why Video LLMs fail and how the proposed defense reallocates attention.
weaknesses: Risk of Over-Refusal on Certain Base Models: For VideoLLaMA3-2B, the False Refusal Rate (FRR) increases noticeably from 0.7% to 13.4% after training with VideoSafety-R1, indicating that less aligned base models are prone to becoming overly defensive.

Template-Constrained Reasoning Quality: The Chain-of-Thought reasoning data in VideoSafetyThinking is generated using fairly rigid prompt templates and commercial LLMs (Qwen-Max). As noted in the limitations, the generated reasoning chains tend to follow stereotyped scripts rather than diverse, human-like deliberative reasoning.

Heavy Reliance on LLM-in-the-Loop Pipelines: The dataset creation (captioning, query generation, filtering) and primary safety evaluation (Qwen-Long) depend heavily on automated LLM/VLM APIs. Although the authors provide reassuring human-model consistency studies in Appendices E and J, automated evaluation can still harbor blind spots against subtle or out-of-distribution adversarial prompts.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely gap in multimodal AI safety: while image-based MLLM safety has been studied, video LLM safety has remained underexplored despite unique vulnerabilities arising from temporal semantics.

Introduces VideoSafetyEval (VSE), a comprehensive, multilingual (10 languages), and systematically constructed benchmark of 11.4k video-query pairs across 19 subcategories, complete with distinct splits (VSE-HH, VSE-SH, VSE-SafeQ) that isolate multimodal safety risks and false refusal behavior.

Provides illuminating empirical findings: demonstrating a severe safety degradation (-34.2% DSR on average) when video input is added to aligned models, and conducting controlled experiments that isolate the impact of semantic complexity from pure token load/frame rate.

Proposes a well-designed defense framework (VideoSafety-R1) combining Alarm Token-Guided SFT (AT-SFT) with dual-modality classification and Safety-guided GRPO with dynamic reward adaptation (DRA), shifting alignment from mere refusal to reasoning-based defense.

Extensive experimental evaluation across 21 Video LLMs, several competitive defense baselines, visual attack benchmarks, and image safety datasets, backed by thorough ablations and mechanistic insights (e.g., attention sink analysis).
Preserves general video understanding performance on diverse benchmarks (MVBench, Video-MME, Perception Test, NextQA) with negligible degradation (<1%).
weaknesses: The reasoning traces in the VideoSafetyThinking (VST) dataset are primarily generated via structured templates with proprietary LLMs (Qwen-Max), which can result in somewhat rigid and formulaic chain-of-thought responses as seen in the qualitative examples.

VideoSafety-R1 causes a noticeable increase in False Refusal Rate (FRR) on VideoLLaMA3-2B (rising from 0.7% to 13.4% on VSE-SafeQ), indicating some residual over-defensiveness on models lacking native RL alignment, though Qwen2.5-VL-3B remains robust.

The core algorithmic components (token injection, multi-task classification heads, and GRPO-based reasoning) synthesize existing paradigms, although their adaptation and dual-modality verification mechanism for video safety are novel and effective.

strengths: Timely and significant problem: Multimodal safety research has predominantly focused on static images, leaving the safety vulnerabilities of video-language models (Video LLMs) under-explored despite rapid deployment.

Comprehensive benchmark (VSE): VideoSafetyEval provides 11.4k video-query pairs spanning 19 subcategories across 10 languages, with well-motivated splits (VSE-HH, VSE-SH, VSE-SafeQ) enabling fine-grained safety, ablation, and false-refusal analysis.

Insightful diagnostic findings: The paper presents an extensive empirical study across 21 Video LLMs showing that incorporating video modality degrades text safety by an average of 34.2%. Controlled experiments (Section 5.5) successfully disentangle token load from semantic richness, revealing that semantic harmfulness and dynamic interactions—rather than sequence length alone—drive the vulnerability.

Effective defense framework (VideoSafety-R1): The combination of Alarm Token-Guided SFT (AT-SFT) and Safety-guided GRPO with dual-modality verification tags and Dynamic Reward Adaptation (DRA) achieves substantial DSR improvements across multiple benchmarks while maintaining general video understanding performance.

Thorough ablation and mechanistic analysis: The paper includes rigorous ablations of each component (alarm tokens, auxiliary classification tasks, GRPO, DRA) and offers interesting mechanistic insights into the visual-to-textual attention sink redistribution.
weaknesses: Templated reasoning traces: The thinking chains generated for the VST dataset (as detailed in Appendix R.7 and the case studies) follow relatively rigid, repetitive prompt templates rather than demonstrating fluid, organic multi-step reasoning.

Reliance on synthetic LLM pipeline: Both dataset creation (video captioning, query generation, filtering) and reference response generation heavily depend on proprietary LLMs (Qwen-Max / Qwen-Max-VL), which could propagate model-specific biases or blind spots.

Reward formulation in GRPO: Incorporating ROUGE as an RL reward alongside verification tags is somewhat restrictive and risk-prone, as ROUGE may encourage lexical overlap with synthetic target answers rather than true safety reasoning and stylistic diversity.

Over-defensiveness in models lacking native RL: While Qwen2.5-VL maintains a low false refusal rate (FRR), VideoLLaMA3-2B suffers a noticeable 12.7% increase in FRR after safety training, pointing to trade-offs in weaker base architectures.
